issues.legal_issue: An application seeking registration after refusal based on denial of execution is not invalid merely because it was labelled as an appeal, if its substance is an application for an inquiry and the parties proceeded on that basis.
material_facts: The Sub-Registrar refused registration after the purported executant denied execution of the sale deed.
The claimant presented the request to the Registrar as an appeal, although an appeal was not available for a refusal based on denial of execution.
The Registrar conducted an inquiry into execution, and both sides participated; the objector invoked the right to question witnesses in that inquiry.
issues.conclusion: The request was not maintainable as an appeal, but its mislabelling did not vitiate the proceedings because, in substance, the Registrar dealt with it as an application for an inquiry and both parties participated on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 72 and 73 of the Registration Act, an appeal is excluded where the Sub-Registrar refuses registration because execution is denied, while a person claiming under the document may apply for an inquiry under Section 73. Sections 74 and 75 prescribe the inquiry and its possible outcome. The substance of the proceeding, rather than its label, governs; the court relied on the commentaries of Mulla and S P Sen Gupta.

rule.if: registration_refusal_proceeding and refusal_based_on_denial_of_execution and request_mislabeled_as_appeal and registrar_conducted_execution_inquiry and both_sides_participated

predicates.registration_refusal_proceeding: A person seeking registration pursued a proceeding before a registration authority after a document was refused registration.
predicates.refusal_based_on_denial_of_execution: The registration officer refused the document because the purported executant denied its execution.
predicates.request_mislabeled_as_appeal: The person seeking registration described the request to the Registrar as an appeal rather than as an application for an inquiry.
predicates.registrar_conducted_execution_inquiry: The Registrar examined whether the document had been executed and whether the registration requirements had been met.
predicates.both_sides_participated: The person disputing execution and the person seeking registration took part in the Registrar's inquiry.

issues.definition: When a registration refusal rests on denial of execution, a wrongly labelled request is not invalidated if the Registrar conducts the relevant inquiry and both sides participate in it.

issues.legal_issue: Admitting a signature on a document does not, by itself, amount to admitting its execution; execution requires signing with assent to terms understood by the signer.
material_facts: The purported executant admitted that her signatures and fingerprints were on the sale deed but disputed having executed it.

She alleged that the deed had been obtained through fraud and undue influence, that its area and boundaries differed from what had been agreed, that it included her residence, and that the full consideration had not been received.
The Registrar relied on evidence that she had signed the deed and affixed her fingerprints, without finding that she understood and assented to its terms.
issues.conclusion: The admission of the signatures and fingerprints did not establish execution of the sale deed; execution required assent to the document's terms after understanding them.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 35(1)(a) and 35(3)(a) of the Registration Act distinguish admitting a signature from admitting execution. Execution means signing as assent to the terms of a document understood by the signer, not merely affixing a signature. The Court relied on Rajendra Pratap Singh v. Rameshwar Prasad, which treated signature as giving rise to a rebuttable presumption of execution; Puran Chand Nahatta v. Monmotho Nath Mukherji, which explains that execution is more than signing; and the reasoning in Suraj Lamps and Industries Private Limited v. State of Haryana and Bharat Indu v. Hakim Mohammad Hamid Ali Khan concerning the purposes of registration. It also considered Section 68 of the Evidence Act and distinguished the definition of execution in Section 2(12) of the Stamp Act because that Act serves a different purpose.

rule.if: document_registration_proceeding and signer_admitted_signature and execution_disputed and (understanding_of_terms_denied or assent_to_terms_denied)

predicates.document_registration_proceeding: A registration authority is deciding whether a document presented for registration was executed.
predicates.signer_admitted_signature: The purported executant acknowledged that the signature on the document was theirs.
predicates.execution_disputed: The purported executant maintained that the document had not been executed by them.
predicates.understanding_of_terms_denied: The purported executant maintained that they did not understand the document's terms when signing it.
predicates.assent_to_terms_denied: The purported executant maintained that they did not agree to be bound by the document's terms.

issues.definition: In a document-registration proceeding, an admitted signature does not establish execution when the purported executant disputes execution and denies understanding or assent to the terms.

issues.legal_issue: A Registrar's summary inquiry into execution cannot resolve a serious, triable dispute about fraud or undue influence in order to direct registration.
material_facts: The purported executant raised disputes about the land area and boundaries in the sale deed, the inclusion of her residence, the consideration, and whether the deed had been procured by fraud and undue influence.
The Registrar relied on evidence of signatures and fingerprints and directed registration without resolving whether the executant understood and assented to the deed's terms.
The executant also produced official inspection reports identifying substantial discrepancies between the land described in the deed and the land found on site.
issues.conclusion: The Registrar exceeded the authority of the summary inquiry by directing registration after adjudicating the disputed issue of fraud and undue influence; the registration order was set aside, leaving the substantive dispute for a competent civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 73 and 74 of the Registration Act authorize an inquiry into whether a document was executed and whether legal requirements for registration were met; Sections 75(1) and 75(4) address the Registrar's power to order registration and summon witnesses. That inquiry is quasi-judicial and summary, not equivalent to a civil trial. A substantive dispute about fraud or undue influence must be adjudicated by a competent civil court. The Court distinguished Satya Pal Anand v. State of M.P., which concerned a challenge to registration after registration had already occurred and the Registrar's lack of power to recall it.

rule.if: registration_inquiry and registrar_ordered_registration and triable_fraud_or_undue_influence_dispute and registrar_resolved_substantive_dispute_in_summary_inquiry

predicates.registration_inquiry: A Registrar conducted an inquiry concerning whether a document presented for registration had been executed.
predicates.registrar_ordered_registration: The Registrar directed that the document be registered.
predicates.triable_fraud_or_undue_influence_dispute: A party raised a substantive dispute that the document was procured by fraud or undue influence and required adjudication on evidence.
predicates.registrar_resolved_substantive_dispute_i: The Registrar decided the substantive fraud or undue-influence dispute as part of the summary registration inquiry.

issues.definition: When a Registrar directs registration after resolving a triable fraud or undue-influence dispute in a summary inquiry, the order exceeds the Registrar's authority.

issues.legal_issue: The availability of a civil remedy does not remove the High Court's power under Article 226 to review whether an order directing registration complied with the governing statutory requirements.
material_facts: The Registrar directed registration of the sale deed after the Sub-Registrar had refused it on the ground that execution was denied.
The executant challenged the Registrar's order by a petition under Article 226, alleging that the registration order was contrary to the statutory limits on the Registrar's inquiry.
The substantive disputes concerning the transaction were also the subject of civil proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could examine whether the Registrar's order directing registration complied with the statutory provisions, notwithstanding the availability of a civil remedy; the Registrar's order in this case was contrary to law and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 permits judicial review of an order directing registration to determine whether the statutory requirements governing the Registrar's power were fulfilled. The existence of a civil remedy to challenge the instrument does not divest the High Court of that jurisdiction, though the High Court retains discretion to decline a writ where disputed factual questions arise. The Court considered Sections 72 to 77 of the Registration Act and distinguished Satya Pal Anand v. State of M.P., which concerned the Registrar's inability to cancel an instrument after it had been registered.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_registration_order: A person affected by a Registrar's direction to register a document challenged that direction in a writ proceeding.
predicates.registrar_directed_registration: The Registrar ordered that a document be registered.
predicates.statutory_compliance_contested: The person challenging the order claimed that the Registrar had acted contrary to the statutory requirements governing registration.

issues.definition: A writ proceeding may review statutory compliance when a person challenges a Registrar's direction to register a document.
